quotes.quote: Jenny Yang, Elizabeth Proehl, Anjan Bharadwaj, Emily Fan, Charlotte Cole, James Kim, Noam Brown, Phoebe Thacker, Amelia Glaese, Tejal Patwardhan OpenAI November 5, 2026
We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks.
representing over $1.7 trillion USD in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories
Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year)
usage metrics don’t capture newer capabilities that take time to adopt, or tasks that users don’t think to ask
we introduce LifeVal, a benchmark explicitly designed to measure AI capabilities on real-world tasks that consumers deeply value.
we used data from the American Time Use Survey (ATUS, 2024; n=7,700) and the Multinational Time Use Study (MTUS, 2020; n=8,782)

The resulting tasks span the most important areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services.
Because no comparable market wage exists for many personal life tasks, we supplemented the ATUS/MTUS task data with a willingness-to-pay survey (n=3,837)
We specified a hypothetical perfect digital superassistant that could provide advice and perform digital tasks, but could not perform physical work.
The resulting data informed a prioritized distribution of 148 activity categories derived from the most detailed level of the ATUS classification
Summing the estimated U.S. annual willingness to pay across these categories yields approximately $1.7 trillion (Table 1).

When writing tasks, expert task writers replaced personally identifiable information (PII) with synthetic data and consented to share their ChatGPT data which itself was de-identified before research use
Our belief is that only an “expert” in the task knows what the truly correct outcome is in the long run for them.
Each task consists of the following components
ChatGPT Conversations and Memories: Relevant excerpts from prior conversations and memories.
Reference Files: Any additional context provided to complete the task in file form
Rubric: To ensure objective grading despite the inherent subjectivity of personalized tasks, writers also create rubrics for each task.
Reinforcement Learning Environment (RLE): Each task has corresponding environment(s) where the model can complete the agentic actions required by the task.
We also give the model a browser tool to search an offline version of the web.
Starting State: Initial data or information required within the environment to complete tasks
LifeVal tasks underwent at least three rounds of human review
Final Sign Off: A third expert reviewer reviewed the completed task and signed off when it was ready for inclusion.
We use two automated graders, both of which use GPT-5.6.
The grader is instructed to score each rubric item independently using only the provided evidence.
We consider any instance when the model accesses internal RLE APIs to be hacking.
If hacking is detected, the sample receives a score of 0.
We created a set of 169 tasks and evaluate GPT-5.2, 5.4, 5.5, 5.6, and GPT-6 Astra.
The plots show 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrapping
GPT-5.2 is the only model to run out of tokens trying to complete the tasks
The most stable failure mode across models is, “Incorrect information or recommendation.”
Models often miss key information that is located in personal conversations.
ATUS ends in 2021, and the most recent survey data from MTUS, which is a database rather than a single survey, is also from 2021.

our willingness-to-pay survey was US-centered and conducted in English, so it may under-represent tasks that are common outside the US or in communities that are weakly represented in demographic survey panels
willingness-to-pay estimates are only a proxy for digital superassistant value
tasks that depend on time-sensitive information or browsing hit a web cache that is not frozen and can therefore change across runs
Points show mean reward for each model setting, with an 8-hour timeout per rollout.
performance versus average observed rollout wall time, average tool calls per rollout, average API cost, and average tokens per rollout
Each bar’s total height is the model’s overall failure rate, computed as the average value of 1 − reward across evaluated samples.

Removed long-tail categories: We excluded work-related activities … and unspecified categories
Recruitment targeted U.S. population distributions for age, gender, ethnicity, and income.
3,837 respondents completed the survey
yielding 1,826 retained respondents and 2,011 exclusions
Each respondent provided valuations for a subset of up to 30 activities from the cleansed ATUS/MTUS task distribution.
We estimated annual willingness to pay for each activity using a 95th-percentile winsorized mean.
Each activity’s share of total estimated willingness to pay across eligible activities was multiplied by a target of 800 tasks and rounded down to the nearest integer.
148 activity categories had positive allocations, corresponding to 702 tasks representing more than $1.7T in annual willingness to pay for US consumers.
we compared our willingness-to-pay rankings against several external proxies for task importance: the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey, O*NET, and the ATUS Wellbeing Survey
These external measures were only moderately correlated with our survey-based … (R2 ≈ 0.4).
Our main grader for the above results was GPT-5.6 Sol with xhigh reasoning.
Seventeen trainers graded one GPT-5.5 rollout for each task in an n=30 subset
the mean rubric grade was 83.61% for humans and 84.20% for GPT-5.6
the Pearson correlation between the mean human grade and the GPT-5.6 grade was r = 0.864
To assess the importance of personalization in LifeVal tasks, we evaluated the tasks under four conditions
We used the same model and varied reasoning effort across all conditions.
Removing additional task context substantially reduced performance at every reasoning effort, while removing past conversations and memories had a much smaller effect.
Past conversations: average win rate of 33.33%.
Memories: average win rate of 47.8%.
Additional task context: average win rate of 55.8%, falling to 41.5% when the information was synthetically inserted into past conversations.
The model has difficulty finding and using relevant information in past conversations.
Participation was voluntary, and contributors could withdraw at any time.
Experts were recruited from existing pools of generalist task writers, supplemented with targeted outreach for niche categories
Measuring AI progress on the tasks that matter in everyday life.
To measure model performance over time on everyday tasks, we built an evaluation of tasks covering areas where users wanted the most help from AI and personal agents.
When someone is looking for help making their life easier, they need more than advice or a chat response.
we started with two large studies that track how people spend time in both the U.S. and internationally
we expanded on these existing surveys with a new demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents

The resulting tasks span the most important areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services.
Below are some examples of how our current models perform on practical workflows from everyday life.
Enroll in the right kindergarten after moving 93.1%
Manage volunteers ahead of a flood 98.0%
Find a new home for my family 100%
Watch a game with grandma from far away 96.3%
Meal prep for a parent adjusting to a new diabetes diagnosis 90.4%
Find a home in Luzerne County that fits my budget, has a separate living unit, and keeps my commute short after school drop-off. Add the deed to my cart
Help me organize our community’s flood preparation volunteer force for four neighbors needing floodproofing assistance.
Help my parent adjust to a new diabetes diagnosis with a practical care and meal plan.
Compare kindergartens near our new home and shortlist the best fits.

That means going beyond academic assessments of model knowledge and actually measuring how well AI models can help people navigate decisions, manage everyday responsibilities, and get meaningful things done.
To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we need to measure and improve model progress on what matters in the lives of everyday people.
Our latest models score very highly on many LifeVal tasks.
Introducing LifeVal, a benchmark measuring how well AI helps people complete everyday tasks, from finding childcare to managing finances and government paperwork.

OpenAI 于 11 月 2 日发布名为 LifeVal 的新基准，用来衡量 AI 模型能否真正帮助普通人完成日常事务
随后又对 3,995 名具有人口代表性受访者开展调查，询问他们最希望个人 AI 助手在哪些事务上提供帮助
不过，LifeVal 目前仍主要是 OpenAI 的内部评估。外界尚未获得完整任务集、评分代码、误差范围或可独立复现的排行榜，因此其结果仍需谨慎解读。
A model is given all task components, including the prompt, personal context, and environment, and attempts to complete the task.
Another model reviews the completion of the task and categorizes failures into rubric, prompt/context, environment, or model-related problems.
Human reviewers assess the model’s proposed fixes and decide whether or not to implement them.
LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks
